note: Source oddity 'the all of the Athenians' carried over as ungrammatical 'the all of the Athenians was set'.
replacement: Meanwhile the two armies on shore, while victory hung in the balance, were a prey to the most agonizing and conflicting emotions. The natives thirsted for more glory than they had already won, while the invaders feared to find themselves in even worse plight than before. Because everything the Athenians had was staked on their fleet, their fear for the outcome was like nothing they had ever felt, and their view of the struggle was necessarily as varied as the battle itself. They were close to the action and were not all looking at the same point at once. Some saw their friends winning, took courage, and called on heaven not to deprive them of safety. Others had their eyes on the losers; they wailed and cried aloud, and though only spectators, they were more overcome than the actual combatants. Others again were gazing at some spot where the battle was evenly disputed. As the struggle dragged on without decision, their swaying bodies reflected the agitation of their minds, and they suffered the worst agony of all, ever just within reach of safety or just on the point of destruction. In short, in that one Athenian army, as long as the sea-fight remained doubtful, every sound was to be heard at once: shrieks, cheers, “We win,” “We lose,” and all the other cries that a great host would necessarily utter in great peril. It was nearly the same with the men in the fleet. At last, after the battle had lasted a long while, the Syracusans and their allies put the Athenians to flight and chased them in open rout to the shore, with much shouting and cheering. The naval force, some one way and some another, ran ashore, all those not taken afloat, and rushed from their ships to the camp. The army was no longer divided but carried away by one impulse, and all deplored what had happened with shrieks and groans. Some ran down to help the ships, others to guard what was left of their wall, while the remaining and most numerous part already began to consider how they should save themselves. Indeed, the panic of that moment had never been surpassed. They now suffered very nearly what they had inflicted at Pylos. Then the Lacedaemonians, with the loss of their fleet, had also lost the men who had crossed over to the island; so now the Athenians had no hope of escaping by land, without the help of some extraordinary accident.
